title: Taiwan's iron window grilles (鐵窗花): their heyday, patterns and decline, and craftspeople and designers who turn the patterns into new objects

facts.text: Iron window grilles reached Taiwan around 1920, together with Western-style modern buildings.
Decorative iron grilles were at their peak from the 1950s to the 1970s, when rising incomes let families build their own houses and care about looks as well as safety.
Grilles on ground-floor windows were mainly meant to keep thieves out; those on upper floors stopped children from falling.
Families also used the grilles for drying clothes, and sunlight through them threw patterns of light on the floor.
Common designs carried wishes: a vase stood for peace, and dragons and phoenixes for good fortune.
Some families had their surname or family hall name worked into the grille, so many grilles were made to order.
Other recorded patterns include mountains, clouds, music notes, palm trees and waves, and simple crosses, diamonds and squares.
Ironworkers used their finest, often brightly painted grilles to show off their skill and attract customers.
The grilles were made of black iron that was cut, bent, forged and welded by hand.
In the past grilles were priced by weight; today hand-made grilles are priced by the days of work plus materials, which makes them much more expensive.
Black iron rusts easily and has to be repainted regularly; a full round of rust removal and painting takes about three weeks.
Stainless steel and aluminum frames, which resist rust, need little care and can be made by machine, gradually replaced hand-made iron grilles.
Some owners removed iron grilles because of worries about escaping from fires, although early makers sometimes built in small doors for escape.
Making grilles by hand is slow, hard to do in large numbers, and welding can harm the eyes over time, so few young people take up the work.
As more old houses are torn down, old grilles are becoming harder to collect; some craftspeople keep antique grilles taken from demolished houses.
Craftspeople and designers now turn grille patterns into small objects such as key-ring charms, picture frames, plant pots, desk lamps, coasters and phone stands.
Grille designs are also used for room dividers, shop signs, table decorations and stair rails.
When an old grille is too rusty to keep, one suggestion is to save part of its pattern and remake it into a decoration instead of throwing the whole grille away.
Customers now often ask for family drawings, pets or other personal symbols to be built into new grille designs.
People who record old houses argue that the skill is not lost; the problem is that hardly anyone wants to use grilles any more, so raising demand is the key to keeping the craft alive.
Because full-size grilles are hard to bring to craft markets, one maker created mini grilles to sell there.
